messages.content: I want to design a persistent ordered index that supports online key-range repartitioning without blocking snapshot scans or compromising crash recovery. Concurrent updates, repartitioning, and crashes must preserve committed writes and snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans. During repartitioning, p99 operation latency must stay within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline.

There are two requirements to satisfy together: correctness while updates, scans, repartitioning, and crashes interact; and a latency bound while repartitioning is underway. The index is persistent and ordered, and changing its key-range partitioning must remain an online activity rather than forcing snapshot scans to wait for repartitioning to finish. For latency, the comparison is specifically p99 operation latency during repartitioning versus p99 operation latency for the same workload without repartitioning, with a limit of 2×.
What does the correctness requirement imply for a range scan that overlaps a range being repartitioned?

The scan must still present one snapshot-consistent view of the requested range. A change in how keys are partitioned must not cause a qualifying key to appear twice in its results, nor cause the scan to mix observations that cannot belong to its snapshot. That is a requirement on what the scan returns, regardless of how the index represents the range internally while repartitioning proceeds.
Does duplicate-free mean the index can never have two internal representations of a key?

Not by itself. The stated requirement is that range scans be duplicate-free. It does not prescribe an internal representation or say whether temporary internal overlap is possible. Whatever representation a design uses, a scan must return each qualifying logical key no more than once while remaining consistent with its snapshot.
And snapshot-consistent means the scan cannot just read whichever version of each key it happens to encounter?

Right. Snapshot consistency calls for the scan’s results to correspond to a coherent snapshot, even if updates and repartitioning occur concurrently. It is not enough to eliminate duplicate keys if the returned values or membership reflect an inconsistent mixture of states. The requirement does not, on its own, specify how the snapshot is selected or represented; the design would need to make its chosen semantics precise.
How should I interpret 'without blocking snapshot scans' alongside that consistency requirement?

Repartitioning must not require snapshot scans to stop and wait for the repartitioning activity to complete. The scans still have to meet their consistency and duplicate-free requirements while it is happening. 'Without blocking' need not mean that a scan takes zero time or has no ordinary operational delay; it means repartitioning cannot depend on suspending snapshot scans as the way to maintain correctness.
What does preserving committed writes add when a crash happens during repartitioning?

A crash must not make committed writes disappear simply because repartitioning was in progress. After recovery, the persistent index must continue to honor those committed writes and support snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans. This speaks to the observable recovery guarantee; it does not dictate a particular persistence or recovery mechanism, or promise that an in-progress scan itself continues through a crash.
So a design cannot handle the crash by picking whichever side of the repartition happens to be easiest if that loses a committed update?

Exactly. Recovery may have to determine what state is valid, but its observable outcome cannot discard a committed write or make range scans inconsistent or duplicative. The requirement applies even when updates, repartitioning, and a crash coincide; it is not limited to crashes at a convenient point between operations.
Is the ordered aspect relevant only to being able to issue a range query?

The goal is an ordered index, so key order matters to the range scans it supports. Repartitioning changes how key ranges are organized, not the logical meaning of their order. A scan over a requested range must still produce a coherent view of that range across any affected partition boundary. The stated goal does not specify the index’s internal structure.
Could I treat scan correctness and write durability as separate checks?

They are distinct properties, but checking each only in isolation would miss the interaction the requirement calls out. A design must preserve committed writes while also providing snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans when updates and repartitioning are concurrent, including after crash recovery. A write being present somewhere is not sufficient if a range scan cannot observe the appropriate logical view of it.
What exactly is compared in the latency requirement?

It compares p99 operation latency during repartitioning with the same workload’s p99 operation latency when repartitioning is not taking place. The former must remain within 2× the latter. It is a relative bound tied to that non-repartitioning baseline, not a fixed time limit and not a comparison against a different workload.
Does the 2× limit apply to every individual operation?

The stated limit is on p99 operation latency, not on every operation’s latency or the maximum latency. An individual operation can exceed the p99 value without, by that fact alone, violating this particular bound. Conversely, meeting the bound requires looking at the p99 comparison for the same workload; a claim about average latency alone would not establish it.
Does staying under that p99 bound make it acceptable to block snapshot scans until repartitioning finishes?

No. Those are separate requirements. Even if an aggregate p99 figure stayed within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline, a design that makes snapshot scans wait for repartitioning to finish would conflict with the nonblocking-scan goal. Likewise, nonblocking scans alone would not establish the p99 bound or the crash-recovery guarantees.
Can I describe the target as a repartition that is transparent to scans?

That is reasonable if 'transparent' is used carefully: snapshot scans should not have to pause for repartitioning, return duplicate keys, or lose their snapshot-consistent view because ranges are being reorganized. It should not be taken to mean repartitioning has no measurable cost, since the goal explicitly allows p99 operation latency during repartitioning of up to 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline.
What should remain unspecified at this point?

The goal sets observable properties, not a particular design. It does not choose a partition representation, a snapshot mechanism, a recovery protocol, or a method for carrying out repartitioning. Those choices would have to be evaluated against the stated contract: committed writes survive the concurrent-update and crash cases; range scans remain snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free, and unblocked by repartitioning; and p99 operation latency during repartitioning stays within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline.
I’d like to explore a design using MVCC B+tree shards, epoch-pinned scan routing, WAL-logged update deltas during bounded background copying, and an atomic partition-map cutover.

Those pieces address different parts of the goal. MVCC B+tree shards provide an ordered, versioned basis for scans. Epoch-pinned routing is intended to keep a scan’s view of partition routing stable while repartitioning proceeds. Bounded background copying moves range contents without making the copy itself a foreground stop-the-world step, while WAL-logged update deltas account for updates that occur during copying. An atomic partition-map cutover gives the change in routing a single logical boundary. This is a proposed design, not yet a demonstration that it meets the correctness and p99 latency requirements.
Why combine MVCC with B+tree shards rather than treating them as the same part of the proposal?

They describe different properties. The B+tree shards describe an ordered index organized into key-range portions. MVCC describes how versions can support reads at a consistent snapshot while writes continue. In the proposal, the shard structure supplies ordered access and MVCC supplies a basis for snapshot visibility; neither term alone explains how scans remain consistent across a repartitioning boundary.
What does epoch-pinned scan routing mean here?

Conceptually, a scan uses a fixed routing epoch for its duration instead of changing partition-map views partway through as repartitioning occurs. That is aimed at preventing a scan from following one routing arrangement for part of its range and another arrangement for the rest. The proposal does not yet specify how an epoch is assigned, how long related state is retained, or how that routing view is coordinated with MVCC visibility.
Is pinning the routing epoch the same as pinning the data snapshot?

No. A routing epoch answers where the scan should look under a particular partition-map view. An MVCC snapshot answers which versions of the data the scan may see. Both need to be coherent for a snapshot-consistent range scan, but they are different kinds of consistency. A stable route alone would not make a scan snapshot-consistent, and a data snapshot alone would not resolve ambiguity if routing changed beneath the scan.
How is the proposal meant to avoid duplicate results across a range that is being copied?

The intended division of responsibility is for epoch-pinned routing to give a scan a consistent way to traverse the range, and for MVCC visibility to determine which logical versions belong in its snapshot. Copying must not make the scan emit the same qualifying logical key twice. The named components point toward that outcome, but the proposal has not specified the exact scan rules needed to establish it.
So an internally copied key would not automatically count as a duplicate scan result?

Correct. The duplicate-free requirement concerns the scan’s observable results, not whether repartitioning temporarily involves more than one internal representation. If the implementation permits overlap while copying, its routing and visibility rules must still ensure that each qualifying logical key appears at most once in the scan. The proposal does not require or rule out a particular internal overlap pattern.
What work is the WAL-logged update-delta part doing?

It addresses the fact that updates can occur while background copying is in progress. Recording those updates as WAL-logged deltas is proposed as a way to make the concurrent changes recoverable and available to be accounted for in the repartitioned state. Merely naming a WAL and deltas does not settle when a write is committed or exactly how deltas and copied data are reconciled; those details matter to preserving committed writes, particularly across a crash.
Does bounded background copying mean the whole repartition has a fixed completion-time bound?

Not as stated. 'Bounded background copying' identifies the copying as bounded work rather than an unbounded foreground interruption, but no particular unit, numerical bound, or completion-time guarantee is given. Its relevance to the goal is that repartitioning should not block snapshot scans and must keep p99 operation latency within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline. Whether the proposed copying behavior achieves that would need to be established, not assumed.
Could the copying be correct while the cutover is still unsafe?

Yes, as a design concern. Having the right contents available does not by itself ensure readers and writers use a coherent partition map when routing changes. The proposed atomic partition-map cutover is meant to make that routing change occur at one logical point rather than exposing a partially changed map. The remaining question is how that boundary interacts with pinned scans, concurrent updates, and crash recovery; the proposal does not yet answer those mechanics.
What should 'atomic' mean for the partition map without assuming a specific implementation?

At the logical level, routing should be observed as being on one side of the cutover or the other, not as a mixture of partially applied partition-map changes. Because this is a persistent index, recovery must also avoid exposing a partial routing change that loses committed writes or breaks scans. That describes the required observable behavior; it does not choose a storage primitive or a protocol for making the cutover durable.
If a scan starts before the cutover and finishes afterward, is that the main reason for the routing pin?

That is one important overlap the pin is intended to address. The scan should not have to stop for the cutover, and changing its routing view midway could complicate duplicate-free coverage of its key range. Keeping one epoch for the scan offers a stable routing view while the map changes for other activity. The proposal still needs rules that make that pinned view usable throughout the scan and consistent with its MVCC snapshot.
What about an update arriving while the background copy is moving its key range?

That is the concurrency case motivating WAL-logged update deltas. The design must account for the committed update even if the range is being copied at the same time; it cannot rely on the copy alone representing a moving set of writes perfectly. The proposal identifies a place for recording concurrent changes, but it does not specify their application order, how they become visible to scans, or how a crash during that process is resolved.
Would WAL logging alone prove that a committed write survives a crash?

No. WAL-logged deltas are a proposed recovery ingredient, not a complete recovery proof. The design must connect the definition of a committed write to what is logged and to the recovered partition-map and data state. Otherwise, it could retain a record yet fail to make the committed write observable through the recovered index. The goal remains to preserve committed writes even when updates, repartitioning, and crashes interact.
How should I judge the p99 requirement for this proposal?

The relevant comparison remains p99 operation latency during repartitioning versus p99 operation latency for the same workload without repartitioning. The repartitioning value must stay within 2× that baseline. Bounded background copying is intended to limit interference, but the proposal supplies no measurements or proof of that limit. Correctness of scans and recovery would not, on its own, establish the latency result.
Is it fair to say the components form a plausible route to the goal, but leave the interactions to be specified?

Yes, with 'plausible' understood as describing the design direction rather than a verified outcome. The proposal names mechanisms for versioned ordered storage, stable scan routing, concurrent-update capture during copying, and a single logical routing cutover. To meet the goal, their interactions must preserve committed writes and snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free, nonblocked range scans across concurrent updates, repartitioning, and crashes, while keeping p99 operation latency during repartitioning within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline.
How can partition splits retain committed writes and duplicate-free snapshot scans through crashes and an atomic cutover?

The central challenge is to make the split look like a change in where a key range is found, not a change in which committed writes exist or what a snapshot scan returns. In the proposed design, background copying and WAL-logged update deltas would have to account for writes made during the split; epoch-pinned routing and MVCC would have to give scans a coherent routing view and data snapshot; and the partition-map cutover would have to change routing atomically. A crash at any point must still leave recovery able to expose committed writes without making scans omit or duplicate qualifying keys. Those are conditions the mechanisms must satisfy, rather than a completed protocol.
What is the most important question to ask about writes during the copy?

For every write considered committed, ask whether it remains represented in a form the index can recover and find, regardless of how far copying has progressed or whether cutover has happened. A copied range by itself might not account for later concurrent writes; that is why the proposal includes WAL-logged update deltas. The unresolved part is precisely how the copied contents, deltas, and routing state are made to agree on what is committed.
Is it enough for recovery to find a committed write somewhere in persistent storage?

No. Preserving it means more than retaining bytes that happen to describe it. The recovered index must make the committed write part of the appropriate logical view of the key range. If routing after recovery could not reach that write, or if a snapshot scan could not observe it when its snapshot calls for it, the observable requirement would not be met.
How does atomic cutover help with that?

It gives the partition-map change a single logical boundary: routing is observed on one side of the cutover or the other, rather than in a partially changed state. That narrows the question for both live operations and recovery. But atomic routing alone does not prove that all committed updates are accounted for on the side the map selects, so it must be coordinated with the copied contents and concurrent-update deltas.
And if a crash occurs right at that boundary?

Recovery must produce a coherent routing view and data state, not expose a partial cutover. Whichever side of the logical cutover recovery makes visible, it must still preserve every committed write and support snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans. The question does not specify the persistence steps that would establish this, so it would be premature to assert how a particular crash-at-cutover case is resolved.
Could a scan simply switch to the new partition map if cutover happens halfway through its range?

An unrestricted switch would need careful justification: a scan could cover one portion under one map and another portion under a different map, risking overlap or a gap in its logical range coverage. The proposed epoch-pinned routing instead aims to keep the scan on one routing view while it runs. That still leaves a necessary condition: the view pinned by the scan must remain usable long enough for the scan to finish without blocking on the split.
Does that pin decide which writes the scan sees?

Not on its own. The routing epoch governs where the scan looks; the MVCC snapshot governs which versions belong in its result. A correct split needs those two views to work together. Stable routing would not excuse showing versions from incompatible snapshots, and consistent version visibility would not excuse traversing a range in a way that emits the same logical key twice.
What does duplicate-free mean if both sides of a split might be relevant internally?

It is a property of the returned range scan, not a requirement that only one internal representation can ever exist. For the scan’s requested range and snapshot, each qualifying logical key must appear no more than once. A design that permits any internal overlap during a split must define scan behavior that prevents that overlap from becoming duplicate results; the question does not specify how that behavior is implemented.
Could avoiding duplicates accidentally hide a committed update?

Yes, that is an important correctness tension to examine. A rule that suppresses a second appearance of a key is insufficient if it also suppresses the version the scan should see, or makes a committed write unreachable after recovery. The desired result is both snapshot-correct membership and values and duplicate-free output, while committed writes remain preserved. Neither property substitutes for the others.
Would checking scans only before and after cutover cover the issue?

No. A scan can overlap the split and the cutover while updates continue. Its pinned routing view and MVCC snapshot must remain coherent for the whole scan, including across the affected key range. Before-and-after observations alone would not address a scan that is already in progress when routing changes.
Should I think separately about a crash before cutover and one after cutover?

Those are useful conceptual cases, along with a crash while the cutover is being made durable. For each case, the same questions apply: what routing view is recovered, where are the committed writes reachable under that view, and can a subsequent range scan produce a snapshot-consistent result without duplicates? This is a way to examine the guarantee, not a claim that a particular recovery procedure has been chosen.
Does the requirement imply that a scan which was running when the system crashed must resume?

No such resume guarantee is stated. The crash-recovery concern is that committed writes remain preserved and that the recovered index can provide snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans. That should not be confused with promising continuity of an individual in-flight scan across a process or system crash.
Where do the WAL-logged deltas fit into the cutover question?

They are the proposed way to account for updates that arrive during bounded background copying. The cutover cannot be judged solely by whether the background copy has moved a range; it must also be judged by whether committed concurrent updates remain recoverable and observable under the routing state exposed afterward. The exact relationship between logging, commitment, copying, and cutover remains to be specified.
Could the partition map be atomic but still disagree with the recovered data?

Conceptually, yes. Atomicity of the map says the routing change is not partially visible. It does not, by itself, say the data reachable through the selected map includes every committed write or that scan visibility is correct. The split must establish agreement between the recovered routing view and the recovered logical contents of the range.
How would you state the proof obligation for a scan spanning the split range?

For a chosen snapshot and requested key range, the scan should cover that logical range under a coherent routing view, return the versions appropriate to its snapshot, and emit each qualifying logical key at most once. It must be able to do so without waiting for repartitioning to finish. The obligation applies even when updates and cutover overlap the scan; after a crash, the recovered index must again support scans with those properties.
And the corresponding proof obligation for writes?

Every committed write must survive the split’s concurrent copying, update handling, cutover, and possible crash, and remain reachable in the recovered logical index. A write cannot be counted as preserved merely because it appeared in one temporary location during repartitioning. The commitment rule and recovery behavior would need to make that guarantee precise.
Is this question answered just by choosing MVCC B+trees and a WAL?

No. Those are components of the proposal, not an automatic proof of their interaction. The open question is whether the split, routing pin, update-delta handling, atomic cutover, and recovery semantics jointly ensure committed writes remain present and scans remain snapshot-consistent and duplicate-free through the relevant concurrency and crash cases.
My hypothesis is that epoch-pinned scans and WAL-ordered delta replay prevent lost commits, snapshot anomalies, and duplicate keys across crash-injected cutovers.

That is a hypothesis about how the proposed split behaves, not an established result. Epoch pinning is intended to keep a scan on a coherent partition-routing view. WAL-ordered delta replay is intended to account for updates made during copying in a recoverable order. Together, they may address the risks around a cutover, but the hypothesis still needs to establish that committed writes remain reachable and that scans return the right snapshot contents without duplicates when crashes are injected around cutover.
Why say 'WAL-ordered delta replay' instead of just saying the deltas are logged?

Logging addresses whether update deltas can be recovered; ordered replay addresses how those recovered changes are applied relative to one another. The hypothesis depends on more than the mere existence of durable records: it proposes that replay respecting WAL order helps preserve the effects of committed updates through a split and crash. It does not specify the full replay procedure or, by itself, prove that the resulting partition state is correct.
What does the epoch pin contribute to the same hypothesis?

It is aimed at the scan side of the problem. If a scan keeps one routing epoch while the partition map cuts over, it need not combine routes selected from different map views partway through its range. That gives the design a basis for avoiding gaps and duplicate coverage. MVCC visibility still has to agree with that routing view; pinning an epoch alone does not establish snapshot consistency.
Could ordered replay prevent a lost commit but leave a duplicate-key problem?

Yes. Recovering a committed update and producing duplicate-free scan results are different obligations. Even if replay retains every committed update, a scan could still emit a logical key twice if its routing or visibility rules expose overlapping representations. The hypothesis says the mechanisms prevent both failures together, which is stronger than saying replay preserves writes.
What exactly counts as a snapshot anomaly here?

In this context, it would be a range-scan result that does not correspond to one coherent MVCC snapshot—for example, treating different parts of the requested range as though they were read at incompatible data views. Duplicate keys are called out separately, though they too would violate the required scan behavior. The hypothesis is that the scan remains snapshot-consistent even when its execution overlaps repartitioning and cutover.
Is an epoch-pinned routing view necessarily an MVCC snapshot?

No. The routing epoch determines which partition-map view the scan follows; the MVCC snapshot determines which key versions it may return. The hypothesis needs those views to be compatible, but it does not make them identical. A stable route with inconsistent version visibility would still produce a snapshot anomaly.
How should I read 'across crash-injected cutovers'? Does it assert that we already ran crash tests?

No. It identifies the failure situation the hypothesis is meant to withstand: crashes deliberately introduced around partition-map cutover. It does not report that any tests have been run or that the hypothesis has passed them. The claimed prevention of lost commits, snapshot anomalies, and duplicate keys remains to be examined under that condition.
Would a crash before cutover and a crash after cutover ask the same correctness question?

They ask the same overarching question under different recovered routing states: are all committed writes still reachable, and can the recovered index produce snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans? The hypothesis is meant to cover cutover-related crash timing, not just an uncomplicated completed split. It does not yet state exactly which partition-map state recovery must choose in any particular case.
What would 'no lost commits' require of replay if copying was still underway?

Every update that was committed must remain represented in the recovered logical index, including updates concurrent with the copy. WAL-ordered delta replay is proposed to help account for those changes, but correctness would depend on how the recovered copy, replayed deltas, and recovered routing view fit together. A committed write existing in a log would not be enough if scans and lookups through the recovered map could not find its logical effect.
Does the hypothesis mean replay must happen before every scan after recovery?

It does not specify that operational sequence. It says WAL-ordered delta replay, together with epoch-pinned scans, prevents the stated failures across crash-injected cutovers. Whatever recovery and scan arrangement is used would have to ensure the observable guarantees, but the hypothesis does not prescribe when replay completes relative to any particular scan.
What if the scan itself overlaps cutover but there is no crash?

The epoch-pinning part is relevant there too: a scan spanning cutover needs a coherent route and a coherent MVCC snapshot without duplicate results. The explicit crash-injected-cutover condition makes the hypothesis more demanding, because recovery must also preserve committed writes and restore a state from which correct scans are possible. It does not imply that an individual scan resumes after a crash.
Am I hypothesizing that replay order alone selects the right partition map?

No. WAL-ordered delta replay concerns concurrent updates; atomic partition-map cutover concerns routing. The hypothesis depends on their interaction, but it does not say replay order alone determines the partition map. A coherent recovered map is still necessary so that the committed effects represented by the copied data and deltas can be reached without duplicate scan output.
Could I phrase the anticipated result as 'every copied key appears exactly once'?

That would be too broad and would shift from logical scan results to internal copying. The relevant expectation is that each key qualifying for a range scan’s snapshot appears once in that scan’s results, with no duplicate keys, while committed writes are retained. Internal representations during copying are not specified by the hypothesis.
Does 'no lost commits' say that uncommitted updates must survive a crash as well?

No. The hypothesis specifically names lost commits, and the underlying requirement is to preserve committed writes. It does not assert that an uncommitted update must become visible after recovery. The distinction matters when assessing whether replay produces the right logical state rather than simply applying every record it can find.
What would keep this from being a complete answer to the partition-split question?

It identifies a proposed explanation, but it does not yet supply the detailed conditions under which an epoch-pinned scan can finish using its routing view, how MVCC visibility is coordinated with that view, or how ordered replay and atomic cutover yield a coherent recovered index. Nor does it provide evidence from crash-injected cutovers. Those gaps are why the statement remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated guarantee.
And this hypothesis does not by itself establish the p99 target, correct?

Correct. It concerns lost commits, snapshot anomalies, and duplicate keys across crash-injected cutovers. It does not establish whether p99 operation latency during repartitioning stays within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline. Correctness under crash and cutover and that latency comparison are separate parts of the overall goal.
So the claim I want to examine is the combined behavior, rather than crediting either mechanism independently?

Yes. The hypothesis is that epoch-pinned scans and WAL-ordered delta replay work together across crash-injected cutovers to prevent all three stated failures: lost commits, snapshot anomalies, and duplicate keys. Showing one mechanism handles one failure mode would not, by itself, establish the combined claim.

I want to turn the partition-split question into a plan: specify WAL commit ordering, replay, and epoch lifetimes; implement a durable partition-map cutover; then crash-test snapshot scans and updates.

That sequence separates the rules the design needs from their implementation and testing. First, specify how WAL commit ordering and replay determine which updates are committed and how they remain represented after recovery. Also specify how long routing epochs remain usable by scans. Then implement a durable map cutover consistent with those rules, and crash-test snapshot scans and updates. This is a plan for establishing the behavior, not a claim that the cutover or tests are complete.
Why put WAL commit ordering in the specification rather than starting with the cutover code?

The cutover needs a precise meaning for 'committed write.' If copying and updates overlap, the design must know which update effects it is obligated to preserve before and after a crash. Specifying WAL commit ordering first gives replay and the durable map cutover a shared rule to follow. The plan does not yet choose the particular ordering rule.
Is commit ordering just the order in which updates arrive?

The plan does not equate those. It calls for WAL commit ordering to be specified: the ordering relevant to determining and recovering committed effects. Arrival order alone would not answer what the system regards as committed or what replay must reproduce. Those meanings still need to be made explicit.
What needs to be specified about replay?

Replay needs a defined relationship to committed updates and to the state selected by the durable partition map. The specification should make clear how recovering logged changes preserves committed writes without making them disappear from the routed key range or appear twice in a snapshot scan. The current plan names replay as work to specify; it does not yet supply an algorithm for it.
Does specifying replay mean deciding that every logged delta must be applied?

Not necessarily. A logged record and a committed write are not automatically the same thing. The replay specification needs to respect whatever commit ordering is defined and produce the appropriate recovered logical state. The plan does not say to apply every record indiscriminately, nor does it set out a rule for which records replay uses.
Why are epoch lifetimes part of this plan?

An epoch-pinned scan needs its routing view to remain usable for as long as the scan relies on it. If a partition-map cutover occurs while a scan is in progress, merely pinning an epoch would not help unless the corresponding routing view remains available for the necessary lifetime. The plan calls for that lifetime to be specified; it does not state a particular duration or retention mechanism.
Is an epoch lifetime a latency limit on the scan?

No. Here it concerns how long a pinned routing view remains valid for a scan. It is not itself a numerical scan-latency target. The overall goal separately requires p99 operation latency during repartitioning to stay within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline, but this plan does not specify a measurement for that requirement.
What does 'durable' add to an atomic partition-map cutover?

Atomicity concerns whether routing appears to change at one logical boundary rather than through a partially visible map. Durability adds the crash question: after recovery, the map must not expose an incomplete cutover that makes committed writes unreachable or breaks snapshot scans. The plan is to implement that durable cutover after the commit, replay, and epoch rules have been specified; it does not name the persistence mechanism.
Could the cutover be durable while replay still gives the wrong result?

Yes, as a correctness possibility to guard against. A consistently recovered map is insufficient if the data and logged updates reachable through that map do not reflect committed writes correctly. That is why the plan includes both replay rules and a durable cutover before testing their combined behavior under crashes.
What should the crash tests tell us about updates?

They should test whether committed updates remain present in the recovered logical index when a crash intersects repartitioning and cutover. Observing that a log record survives would not alone settle the question; the write needs to be reachable through the recovered index. The plan says to crash-test updates, but it does not report any test outcome.
And what should they tell us about snapshot scans?

They should test whether the index supports snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free range scans in the relevant crash and recovery cases, while scans that run during repartitioning are not blocked by it. A useful observation is the scan’s logical result, not merely whether it completes: the returned keys and versions must fit one snapshot without duplicate keys. The plan does not yet define test cases or claim those observations have been made.
Am I planning to resume an individual scan after a crash?

That is not stated. Crash-testing snapshot scans can examine scan behavior around repartitioning and the ability of the recovered index to serve correct scans. It need not imply that an in-flight scan survives and resumes across a crash. The stated goal concerns preservation of committed writes and correct snapshot scans, not resumption of a particular interrupted request.
Why test scans and updates together instead of treating them as unrelated checks?

The difficult interaction is that updates can be committed while a key range is being repartitioned and scans are using a snapshot and a pinned routing view. After a crash, preserving a write is not enough if a scan cannot find its appropriate version; avoiding duplicate scan results is not enough if a committed update was lost. Testing both aspects is intended to examine the combined observable behavior.
Does this plan already specify the exact moment at which cutover becomes committed?

No. It calls for specifying WAL commit ordering and replay, and for implementing a durable map cutover, but it does not define an exact cutover-commit point. That relationship would need to be made precise in the specification and implementation rather than inferred from the word 'durable.'
Could I implement the cutover first and work out epoch lifetimes afterward while keeping the same plan?

That would change the stated sequence. The plan is to specify WAL commit ordering, replay, and epoch lifetimes, then implement the durable map cutover, then crash-test snapshot scans and updates. Epoch lifetime rules are relevant to what a cutover must allow an already-pinned scan to do, so they belong in the specification stage as stated.
Does 'then crash-test' mean the tests only matter after implementation?

In this plan, crash-testing follows implementation of the durable cutover, so the tests can exercise the resulting behavior. That ordering does not claim that a design becomes correct just because it has been implemented, or that the later tests have already occurred. It identifies the intended progression from specified rules to implementation to examination under crashes.
Should the specification distinguish routing-epoch lifetime from MVCC-version visibility?

Yes, conceptually. An epoch lifetime says how long a scan can use a particular partition-routing view; MVCC visibility says which data versions belong to its snapshot. The plan explicitly calls for epoch lifetimes to be specified, and a crash test of snapshot scans would need a clear notion of correct snapshot results. The plan does not collapse those two views into one or prescribe their precise coordination.

That proposes a post-recovery allocation of read I/O while split-related work resumes. Scans receive a 75% reservation, resumed split-delta replay has a 25% cap, and cutover is deferred. Why is 'after mandatory recovery' important to the wording?

It sets the sequence. The 75% scan reservation and 25% cap apply after mandatory recovery, when split-delta replay resumes. The proposal does not say that those percentages govern mandatory recovery itself, or specify precisely what mandatory recovery entails.
Should I describe resumed split-delta replay as mandatory recovery?

Not interchangeably. The proposal distinguishes mandatory recovery from the resumed split-delta replay that is capped afterward. It does not define every operation in either phase, so the distinction should be preserved rather than assuming they are identical.

It assigns that share of read-I/O capacity to scans under the proposed policy. It does not promise that scans always use all 75%, that an individual scan completes within a particular time, or that reserving capacity alone makes its result snapshot-consistent.
And how should I read the 25% figure?

It is a cap on resumed split-delta replay, not a promise that replay will continuously consume 25%. Read alongside the scan reservation, it limits replay's claim on read I/O after mandatory recovery. The proposal does not define the accounting interval or an enforcement mechanism.
Since 75% and 25% add to 100%, can I say every unit of read I/O is always consumed by one of those two activities?

No. A reservation and a cap describe an allocation policy, not actual utilization. Scans may not need their entire reservation at every moment, and replay may use less than its cap. The proposal does not specify how unused capacity is handled.
Does the 25% replay cap also limit how much WAL data can exist?
No. The cap concerns resumed split-delta replay's use of read I/O after mandatory recovery. It is not a limit on log size, the number of update deltas, or which committed writes must be preserved.
Could limiting replay permit us to ignore some committed update deltas?

No. Capping resource use changes the pace at which resumed split-delta replay proceeds; it cannot relax the requirement to preserve committed writes. The proposal does not specify the replay procedure, but any resulting index state must still account for committed updates.
Does the 75% scan reservation mean snapshot scans are correct even if replay is incomplete?

No. Available read I/O and correct results are separate concerns. Scans still need a snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free view, and committed writes must remain represented. The proposal does not specify how scans and incomplete split-delta replay interact to deliver that view.
What role does deferring cutover play here?

It postpones the partition-map routing transition while the proposed post-recovery read-I/O allocation is in effect. That avoids treating cutover as something that must happen immediately when split-related work resumes. The proposal does not state the condition for proceeding with cutover or how its durability is implemented.
Is 'defer cutover' a decision to abandon the split?
No. Deferring a cutover means putting it off, not canceling it. The proposal gives no deadline for the eventual cutover or guarantee about how quickly the split completes.
Can I infer that cutover occurs as soon as split-delta replay reaches the 25% cap?

No. The cap is a limit on replay's resource use, not a cutover trigger. The proposal does not specify a cutover condition, and reaching a resource cap would not by itself establish that a partition-map transition is ready.
Does deferring cutover mean snapshot scans must wait?

No. The index's goal is to avoid blocking snapshot scans during repartitioning. Deferring cutover is a routing decision about when the transition occurs; it is not permission to suspend scans. Could the policy satisfy scan latency by deferring cutover indefinitely?

That would not establish a satisfactory online repartition: a split that never reaches cutover has not completed its routing transition. What latency comparison would tell us whether this proposal helps with the performance goal?

Measure p99 operation latency during the relevant repartitioning condition against p99 for the same workload without repartitioning; the goal requires the former to stay within 2× the latter. Post-recovery scan p99 under the proposed reservation is particularly relevant, but the proposal contains no p99 measurement or assertion that the limit is met.
Would a scan p99 at exactly 2× its same-workload baseline meet that threshold?
Yes. 'Within 2×' includes equality. That interpretation of the threshold is not a prediction of what the 75% reservation and 25% replay cap will achieve.
Is reserving 75% for scans the same as guaranteeing the overall p99 operation-latency bound?

No. A resource allocation might affect scan latency, but the requirement concerns observed p99 operation latency compared with a same-workload non-repartitioning baseline. The proposal also does not specify a separate reservation for foreground updates, so the percentages alone cannot establish the overall operation-latency result.
Does this proposal say foreground updates stop while replay resumes?

No. It allocates read I/O between scans and resumed split-delta replay after mandatory recovery, and it defers cutover. It does not prescribe stopping updates or define their resource allocation. Concurrent updates must still be handled without losing committed writes.
What happens if another crash occurs while replay is capped?

The recovery requirement still applies: committed writes must be preserved and the recovered index must support correct scans. The proposal does not describe how replay progress or the deferred cutover state is made durable across another crash. The 25% cap, by itself, is not a recovery protocol.

The proposal does not establish that claim. Deferring the routing transition and selecting a coherent partition-map generation for a scan are related concerns, but the read-I/O policy does not specify the scan-routing rule. Snapshot-consistent, duplicate-free scans remain necessary regardless of when cutover occurs.

They are proposed allocation values: reserve 75% of read I/O for scans and cap resumed split-delta replay at 25%. They are not reported measurements of how much I/O either activity actually used.

The post-mandatory-recovery policy would need to be assessed on its stated trade-offs: whether scans remain correct and unblocked, committed writes survive crashes and replay, p99 operation latency stays within 2× the same workload's non-repartitioning baseline, and deferring cutover does not prevent the split from completing. My hypothesis is that, for uncutover splits, recovered parent shards contain every committed write and support snapshots while child-delta replay is paused.

Is that saying a copied child shard cannot contain those writes too?

What role does pausing child-delta replay play in the claim?

It makes the claim stronger than one that relies on replay finishing before snapshots are served. The hypothesis predicts that, for uncutover splits, pausing child-delta replay does not prevent the recovered parent shards from containing committed writes or supporting snapshots. It does not say replay may be omitted permanently.
Can I conclude from this that child-delta replay never matters to committed-write preservation?

No. The claim is scoped to uncutover splits and the interval when child-delta replay is paused. It does not state what replay must do to prepare child ranges, complete the split, or handle a later cutover.
Does a paused replay mean the system is still in the middle of mandatory recovery?

The hypothesis does not equate the two. It concerns recovered parent shards supporting snapshots while child-delta replay is paused. It does not define the boundary of mandatory recovery or claim that snapshots can be served before whatever mandatory recovery requires has completed.
What should “support snapshots” mean for a range scan?

The recovered parent state must provide the versions appropriate to a scan’s snapshot, not merely contain a current value for each key. Under the index’s correctness goal, range scans must also be duplicate-free. The hypothesis proposes that the parent shards can serve snapshots in the stated paused-replay condition; it does not spell out the scan algorithm.
Would seeing every committed key in the parent prove that snapshot support works?

If a parent and child both contain a key while replay is paused, what keeps a scan duplicate-free?

The hypothesis does not give an explicit routing or deduplication rule. It says recovered parent shards support snapshots for uncutover splits; satisfying the broader scan requirement would mean a range scan returns each qualifying logical key no more than once. The possible presence of a child copy does not, on its own, tell us which representation a scan traverses.
Are we assuming that a snapshot scan reads from both the parent and the child?

No. The hypothesis emphasizes the recovered parent shards as sufficient to support snapshots while child-delta replay is paused. It does not require a scan to read child ranges, nor does it specify that scans are forbidden from doing so. The routing behavior would need to be made precise to assess the claim.
Could a write be committed in a log but not yet represented in the recovered parent?

If that happened in an uncutover split, it would challenge this hypothesis: it predicts that the recovered parent shards contain every committed write. The statement does not explain the recovery steps that ensure the parent reflects committed log records, so that connection remains something to establish.
Does this imply that pausing replay makes recovered writes disappear from the child?

No. Pausing child-delta replay describes a halt in that work, not deletion of child contents. The hypothesis concerns whether the recovered parent state remains sufficient for committed writes and snapshots during the pause; it makes no claim about removing or retaining particular child representations.
If another crash occurs during the pause, can I assume the hypothesis still holds?

Whether repeated recovery actually preserves that condition is not demonstrated by the hypothesis.
Is a scan interrupted by that crash supposed to resume?

No scan-resumption guarantee is stated. Supporting snapshots means the recovered index can serve appropriate snapshot views in the specified condition; it does not say an individual in-flight scan survives a crash.
How does this relate to the proposal to defer cutover?

For that approach to rely on paused child-delta replay, the recovered parent shards would need to retain every committed write and support snapshots during the pause. This states a necessary claim to examine, not a verified consequence of deferring cutover.
Would the hypothesis allow cutover immediately, before replay resumes?

It does not address that case. The claim is expressly about uncutover splits. It supplies no readiness criterion for cutover and no guarantee that child ranges are prepared to serve snapshots while their delta replay is paused.
Does retaining writes in the parent say anything about how long the split takes to finish?

No. It is a correctness hypothesis about recovered contents and snapshot support during paused replay. It gives no split-completion time or assurance that a prolonged pause would allow cutover to proceed.
Does it establish the 2× p99 latency requirement?

No. Serving snapshots from recovered parent shards while child-delta replay is paused is not itself a latency measurement. The requirement that p99 operation latency during repartitioning stay within 2× the same workload’s non-repartitioning baseline remains separate.

What if a key has several committed versions?

Would a duplicate-free scan prove that all committed versions are available?

No. A scan can avoid duplicate keys while returning an inappropriate version or omitting one its snapshot requires. Duplicate-free output remains necessary, but it does not establish the parent shards’ ability to serve every committed version.
If the parent serves the right versions, does that automatically settle duplicate-free range scans?

Not automatically. The scan must also follow a coherent routing view and emit each qualifying logical key at most once. Version availability in the parent addresses one part of snapshot correctness; it does not alone define how a range scan traverses a split.
Could the parent be sufficient for snapshots while the child replay is paused, but the split still be unable to finish?

Does it say how long child replay stays paused?
